Start here

You will meet five patients. For each one, read the story, talk it through with your group, then open the explanations and test yourself at each checkpoint. Your progress is saved on this device.

By the end you should be able to

  1. Define and give examples of labile, stable and permanent cells, and explain how their capacity to divide shapes the way a tissue adapts.
  2. Define hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy and metaplasia, with physiological and pathological examples of each.
  3. Outline the main mechanisms behind each adaptation.
  4. Recognise these adaptations in gross and microscopic images and link them to a clinical scenario.
  5. Explain how dysplasia differs from metaplasia, and define aplasia, hypoplasia, hamartoma and choristoma.

Stress, adaptation and injury

What is an adaptation?

A reversible change in the size, number, phenotype, metabolic activity or function of cells in response to a change in their environment. The cell reaches a new steady state and keeps working.

When adaptation fails

If the stress is too severe, or the cell can no longer adapt, it moves into reversible injury, then irreversible injury and cell death (necrosis or apoptosis).

Cells differ in their ability to divide

Labile cells

Divide continuously throughout life. e.g. bone marrow, surface epithelia of skin, GIT, cervix

Stable cells

Quiescent (G0) but re-enter the cycle when stimulated. e.g. liver, kidney tubules, fibroblasts, smooth muscle

Permanent cells

Cannot divide in postnatal life. e.g. neurons, cardiac muscle, (mostly) skeletal muscle

Why it matters

Only tissues with dividing cells can undergo hyperplasia. Tissues made of permanent cells respond to extra demand by hypertrophy alone.

Checkpoint

A 34-year-old man donates the right lobe of his liver to his brother. Three months later a CT scan shows that his remaining liver has almost regained its original volume. Which statement best explains this?

Hepatocytes are stable cells. They sit in G0 but re-enter the cell cycle after partial hepatectomy, driven by growth factors (e.g. HGF) and cytokines. This is compensatory hyperplasia.

They are not permanent (they can divide) and not labile (they do not divide continuously). Metaplasia swaps one cell type for another, and fatty change is injury, not growth.

Case 1 · Hypertrophy

CASE 1

Encik Rahman, 58, company manager

Encik Rahman has had high blood pressure for 15 years. He often forgets his tablets and his readings are usually around 170/100 mmHg.

Over the past year he gets breathless climbing two flights of stairs. His ECG shows tall QRS complexes, and an echocardiogram reports a thick-walled left ventricle.

Six months later he develops sudden, crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm. He dies in the ICU despite treatment, and an autopsy is done.

Discuss in your group

  • What change would you expect in the size of his heart? Why?
  • Can cardiac muscle cells divide to cope with the extra workload?
  • Why might a thickened heart be more vulnerable to ischaemia?

The autopsy

Left ventricular hypertrophy (concentric) due to systemic hypertension

The LV wall is markedly thickened and the cavity looks small. Myocytes cannot divide, so the whole increase comes from larger cells, not more cells.

Hypertrophy

Key points

  • An increase in the size of cells, which increases the size of the organ.
  • No new cells, just bigger ones.
  • Due to synthesis of more structural proteins and organelles, not cell swelling.
  • Seen where cells cannot divide. In tissues that can divide it often occurs together with hyperplasia.

Physiological

  • Uterus in pregnancy: oestrogen drives smooth muscle hypertrophy (and hyperplasia).
  • Skeletal muscle of weightlifters and athletes.

Pathological

  • Left ventricle in systemic hypertension or aortic stenosis.
  • Right ventricle in pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease.

How does a myocyte get bigger?

Mechanism

  1. Triggers: mechanical stretch, growth factors (e.g. IGF-1) and agonists (e.g. angiotensin, α-adrenergic hormones).
  2. Signalling: e.g. PI3K/AKT and G-protein-coupled receptor pathways.
  3. Transcription factors (GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) switch on genes for contractile proteins.

Myocytes may also switch to fetal forms of contractile proteins (β-myosin heavy chain) and make atrial natriuretic peptide.

When adaptation turns into injury

Back to Encik Rahman

Hypertrophy has a limit. The thick ventricle needs more oxygen, while hypertension also damages the coronary arteries. The mismatch between supply and demand made a myocardial infarction more likely.

Adaptation, injury and cell death sit on one continuum.

Checkpoint

A 24-year-old national-level weightlifter has a pre-competition ECG showing increased QRS voltage. Echocardiography shows a symmetrically thickened left ventricular wall with normal function. Which change in his cardiac muscle cells best explains this?

This is physiological hypertrophy. Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells, so they respond to extra workload by making more contractile protein and getting bigger.

Mitosis does not add new myocytes in adults. Water influx is cell swelling, an early sign of injury. Fibrosis follows myocyte death, and lipofuscin is the "wear and tear" pigment of atrophy.

Case 2 · Hyperplasia

CASE 2

Mr Lim, 71, retired teacher

Over two years Mr Lim has noticed that his urinary stream is weak and he has to strain to start. He passes urine every 2 hours in the day and gets up four times at night.

On rectal examination his prostate is enlarged, smooth, firm and rubbery, with no hard nodules. His PSA is mildly raised. He undergoes a transurethral resection of the prostate.

Discuss in your group

  • Is the prostate bigger because its cells are larger or because there are more of them?
  • Which hormone drives this change?
  • Does this condition turn into prostate cancer?

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (nodular hyperplasia)

More glands and more stromal cells, driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT). The nodules surround the urethra and obstruct urine flow. BPH does not raise the risk of prostate cancer.

Hyperplasia

Key points

  • An increase in the number of cells in an organ or tissue.
  • Only possible where cells can divide (labile and stable cells).
  • Often happens together with hypertrophy.
  • It is controlled: it stops when the stimulus is removed, which separates it from a neoplasm.

Mechanism

Growth factor-driven proliferation of mature cells, and in some cases more output of new cells from tissue stem cells. The stimuli are hormones, growth factors and cytokines.

Physiological

Hormonal: breast epithelium at puberty, pregnancy and lactation; uterus in pregnancy.

Compensatory: liver after partial hepatectomy; bone marrow after blood loss.

Pathological

  • Endometrial hyperplasia: excess oestrogen relative to progesterone.
  • BPH: androgen (DHT) stimulation.
  • Skin warts: growth factors from papillomaviruses.
  • Goitre: TSH-driven thyroid hyperplasia.

Endometrial hyperplasia raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma; BPH does not raise the risk of prostate cancer.

Checkpoint

A 49-year-old obese woman with irregular, anovulatory cycles has heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding. An endometrial biopsy shows crowded, back-to-back glands without cellular atypia. What is the most likely cause, and why does it matter?

Fat converts androgens to oestrogen, and anovulation means no progesterone to oppose it. The result is pathological endometrial hyperplasia, which can progress to endometrial carcinoma if the stimulus continues.

Atrophy follows loss of oestrogen. Crowded glands mean more cells, so this is hyperplasia, not hypertrophy or metaplasia.

Case 3 · Atrophy

CASE 3

Puan Aminah, 76, grandmother of nine

Puan Aminah had a stroke eight months ago that left her right arm and leg paralysed. She has been bedbound since, eats poorly and has lost 9 kg.

Her daughter says she had been getting more forgetful for several years before the stroke. Her right calf and forearm are now visibly thinner than the left. She dies of pneumonia, and an autopsy is performed.

Discuss in your group

  • Why are her right limb muscles smaller? List every cause you can find in the story.
  • What would you expect her brain to look like?
  • Is this change reversible?

Cerebral atrophy

Narrow gyri and wide sulci; the brain is lighter. Causes here: ageing and reduced blood supply (atherosclerosis). Her limb muscles shrank from disuse, loss of innervation and poor nutrition, all at once.

Atrophy

Definition

A reduction in the size of an organ or tissue from a decrease in cell size and number. The cells are smaller but alive, with fewer organelles and lower function.

Physiological

  • Notochord and thyroglossal duct in fetal life
  • Uterus after childbirth
  • Endometrium and breast after menopause
Pathological causeExample
Decreased workloadLimb in a plaster cast; bed rest
Loss of innervationMuscle after nerve injury or stroke
Reduced blood supplyBrain in atherosclerosis
Poor nutritionMalnutrition, cancer cachexia
Loss of hormonal stimulationEndometrium, breast after menopause
PressureTissue around a slowly growing benign tumour

↓ Protein synthesis

Less protein is made with reduced workload, metabolic activity or growth signals.

↑ Protein degradation

Mainly through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.

Autophagy

Starved cells digest their own components in autophagic vacuoles. Undigested residues remain as lipofuscin, which colours the organ brown (brown atrophy).

Checkpoint

A 25-year-old footballer has his right leg in a plaster cast for 8 weeks after a tibial fracture. When the cast is removed, his right calf is clearly thinner than the left. Nerve conduction studies are normal. What is the main mechanism behind the change?

This is disuse atrophy. Less work means less protein synthesis and more degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, so the fibres shrink. It reverses with physiotherapy.

There is no necrosis, and the fibres are smaller rather than lost. Metaplasia means a change of cell type. Normal nerve conduction rules out denervation.

Case 4 · Metaplasia

CASE 4

Mr Kumar, 46, lorry driver

Mr Kumar has smoked about 30 cigarettes a day since he was 16. For five years he has had a cough with sputum most mornings, and he gets frequent chest infections.

Bronchoscopy shows inflamed bronchial mucosa. A biopsy is taken from the main bronchus.

Discuss in your group

  • What is the normal lining of the bronchus, and what does it do?
  • How might that lining change in a heavy smoker?
  • Why does he keep getting chest infections?

Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium

Ciliated columnar epithelium has been replaced by stratified squamous epithelium, which survives smoke better. The price: no cilia and less mucus, so mucociliary clearance is lost and infections are more common.

Metaplasia

Definition

A reversible change in which one differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another. The new cells cope better with the hostile environment, but some protective function is lost.

Mechanism

Reprogramming of tissue stem (reserve) cells, or colonisation by differentiated cells from nearby, driven by cytokines, growth factors and matrix signals. Retinoic acid helps control the switch, which is why vitamin A deficiency causes squamous metaplasia.

A double-edged sword

If the stimulus persists, the same influences can lead to malignant transformation. Squamous metaplasia in the bronchus can precede squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

CASE 4b

Mrs Tan, 54, shopkeeper

Mrs Tan has had heartburn and acid regurgitation for over 10 years, worse after meals and at night. She buys antacids over the counter.

Endoscopy shows a salmon-pink, velvety tongue of mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. A biopsy is taken.

Discuss in your group

  • What is the normal lining of the lower oesophagus?
  • What has replaced it here, and why?
  • What is the long-term risk?

Barrett oesophagus: intestinal (columnar) metaplasia

Chronic acid reflux has replaced the stratified squamous lining with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. It is the main precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so these patients need endoscopic surveillance.

TypeExamplesCancer that may follow
Squamous (columnar → squamous)Bronchus in smokers; vitamin A deficiency; stones in salivary, pancreatic or bile ducts; cervical transformation zoneSquamous cell carcinoma
Columnar (squamous → columnar)Barrett oesophagus in chronic acid refluxAdenocarcinoma
Connective tissueBone forming in muscle after a bleed (myositis ossificans)Not a recognised precursor
Checkpoint

A 57-year-old man with 15 years of untreated reflux has an endoscopy showing a salmon-pink area of mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Which biopsy finding confirms the likely diagnosis, and which tumour is he at risk of?

This is Barrett oesophagus: squamous mucosa replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. It is the main precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

Squamous carcinoma arises from squamous mucosa. Ciliated epithelium belongs to the airway. Lymphoma and bone formation are not features of reflux.

Case 5 · Beyond adaptation

CASE 5

Mr Kumar, 8 years later

Mr Kumar never stopped smoking. He now has blood-streaked sputum. A repeat bronchial biopsy shows squamous epithelium in which the cells vary in size and shape, nuclei are large and dark, mitoses are seen above the basal layer and the normal layering is lost. The basement membrane is intact.

Dysplasia

Disordered growth with loss of uniformity of cells and loss of architectural orientation: pleomorphism, hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei, misplaced mitoses and loss of maturation.

Dysplasia is not an adaptation; it is a pre-neoplastic change. Mild dysplasia may regress if the cause is removed. Full-thickness dysplasia is carcinoma in situ, and once the basement membrane is breached it becomes invasive carcinoma.

Developmental disorders of growth

Failure to develop

  • Agenesis: complete absence of an organ and its primordium.
  • Aplasia: the organ fails to develop; only a rudiment remains.
  • Hypoplasia: the organ forms but never reaches full size.
  • Atresia: failure of a lumen to form (e.g. oesophageal atresia).
HamartomaChoristoma
What it isDisorganised mass of tissues native to that siteNormal tissue in the wrong place (heterotopia)
ExampleLung hamartoma: cartilage and bronchial epitheliumPancreatic tissue in the wall of the stomach
NatureMalformation, not a true neoplasm (some carry clonal changes)Malformation, not a neoplasm
Checkpoint

A 60-year-old smoker has a bronchial biopsy. The squamous epithelium shows cells of varying size and shape with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei, mitoses above the basal layer and loss of orderly maturation. The basement membrane is intact. Which term best describes this?

Pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, misplaced mitoses and loss of maturation are the features of dysplasia, a pre-neoplastic change.

Metaplasia and hyperplasia produce normal-looking cells. An intact basement membrane rules out invasion. A hamartoma is a malformed mass of native tissue.

Self-assessment

Eight more questions, several based on images you have already seen.

Self-assessment

A 72-year-old man with nocturia has this prostate removed. What is the process, and which hormone drives it?

The nodular cut surface with compressed urethra is benign prostatic hyperplasia. DHT, made from testosterone by 5α-reductase, drives proliferation of glands and stroma.

Carcinoma is usually hard and peripheral, not this nodular transition-zone pattern. Both glands and stroma increase in number, so it is hyperplasia.

Self-assessment

This is the brain of an 80-year-old woman with long-standing memory loss and generalised atherosclerosis (right) compared with a normal brain (left). Which statement is correct?

Narrow gyri and wide sulci show cerebral atrophy, here from ageing and reduced blood supply.

Neurons are permanent cells and cannot undergo hyperplasia. Metaplasia and hamartoma do not fit.

Self-assessment

This is cardiac muscle from an elderly patient with cancer cachexia. What is the pigment, and what does it represent?

Fine yellow-brown granules next to the nuclei are lipofuscin, the "wear and tear" pigment left over from autophagy. In bulk it gives brown atrophy.

Haemosiderin is iron and stains with Prussian blue. Melanin, bilirubin and carbon do not collect in atrophic myocytes in this way.

Self-assessment

A 55-year-old man with chronic heartburn has this endoscopic appearance (right). Biopsy is most likely to show:

Salmon-pink mucosa above the GE junction in a reflux patient is Barrett oesophagus, an intestinal (columnar) metaplasia.

It is a precursor of adenocarcinoma, not squamous carcinoma. Ciliated epithelium and hamartoma do not fit.

Self-assessment

This section is from the left ventricle of a man with long-standing aortic stenosis. Which statement about these cells is true?

Large myocytes with big, dark "boxcar" nuclei are hypertrophied. Pressure overload makes them build more contractile protein.

Myocytes are permanent cells, so they cannot divide. Swelling is injury, and squamous change is metaplasia of epithelium.

Self-assessment

A child in a famine-affected area has night blindness and recurrent chest infections. Which change in the bronchial lining is most likely?

Retinoic acid is needed to keep normal columnar differentiation. In vitamin A deficiency, respiratory epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia, and the night blindness gives the clue.

Acid reflux affects the oesophagus, not the bronchi. The other options do not follow from vitamin A deficiency.

Self-assessment

During a gastrectomy for an ulcer, the surgeon finds a 1 cm nodule in the stomach wall. Histology shows normal pancreatic acini and ducts. What is it?

Normal tissue in an abnormal location is a choristoma (heterotopic pancreas).

A hamartoma is made of tissues native to the site. Metaplasia replaces one cell type with another in place; this is a developmental rest.

Self-assessment

A 30-year-old woman from an iodine-deficient area has a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland with normal thyroid function tests. What best explains the enlargement?

Low iodine reduces hormone output, so TSH rises and stimulates hyperplasia (and hypertrophy) of follicular cells to keep the patient euthyroid. This is a diffuse goitre.

Atrophy would shrink the gland. Metaplasia and choristoma do not fit, and C cells are not driven by iodine deficiency.

Summary

AdaptationWhat changesPhysiologicalPathological
Hypertrophy↑ Cell sizeWeightlifter's muscle; pregnant uterusLV in hypertension (Encik Rahman)
Hyperplasia↑ Cell numberLactating breast; liver regrowthBPH (Mr Lim); endometrial hyperplasia
Atrophy↓ Cell size and numberPost-partum uterus; menopauseDisuse, denervation, ischaemia (Puan Aminah)
MetaplasiaOne cell type replaced by anotherCervical transformation zoneBronchus in smokers (Mr Kumar); Barrett (Mrs Tan)

Take-home messages

  • All four adaptations are reversible if the stimulus is removed.
  • Which one happens depends on the stimulus and on whether the cells can divide.
  • Dysplasia is not an adaptation; it is a step towards cancer.

Reference: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC, Deyrup AT. Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 11th ed. Elsevier; 2023. Chapter 1.
